v.

EDDIE GRANT, JR., et al.,
Petitioners,
v.
RONNELL HIGGINS, IN HIS OFFICIAL CAPACITY
AS COMMISSIONER OF THE CONNECTICUT
DEPARTMENT OF EMERGENCY SERVICES AND
PUBLIC PROTECTION, et al.

ON WRITS OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURTS OF APPEALS
FOR THE SEVENTH AND SECOND CIRCUITS

BRIEF FOR THE
CONNECTICUT RESPONDENTS

INTRODUCTION
On December 14, 2012, a lone gunman armed with
an AR -15-style rifle murdered twenty first -graders
and six educators inside Sandy Hook Elementary
School in Newtown, Connecticut.  It was the deadliest
elementary school shooting in American history, and
the m assacre was committed in less than five
minutes—before police could even respond.

2
Connecticut’s elected representatives acted swiftly
following this tragedy.  Within months, Connecticut
enacted a bipartisan law that aimed to prevent a massacre like Sandy Hook from ever happening again
within the State.  A key provision of that law prohibited the very AR -15-style weapons that made the
Sandy Hook mass shooting so deadly.
That AR- 15 ban is “consistent with the Nation’s
historical tradition of firearm regulation.”  N.Y. State
Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1, 24 (2022).
From fourteenth-century England to twenty-first century America, governments have restricted weapons
because of their unusually dangerous properties.  And
although the weapons have evolved —from the
launcegay to the Bowie knife to the Tommy gun—the
rationale behind those laws has not.  In each instance,
legislatures have determined that a weapon is atypically lethal relative to its peers —and so have acted to
prevent that weapon’s use.
In making that same judgment as to AR -15s, Connecticut’s law closely matches its  “historical precursors.”  United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 692
(2024).  Among commercially available weapons, the
AR-15 is distinctively capable of swiftly inflicting fatal
injuries on a scale  similar to its military counterpart,
the M-16.  That capacity for lethality comes from a mix
of features that permit even an unskilled gunman to
rapidly fire high -velocity bullets that leave catastrophic wounds.  Tragically, real- world experience
confirms the AR -15’s singular dangerousness: From
Sandy Hook to Las Vegas to Parkland to Uvalde,
shooters have used the AR -15 or similar weapons in
the vast majority of mass-casualty shootings this century.  So too, AR -15s have been used to kill law -enforcement officials at a sharply disproportionate

3
rate—including in Bristol, Connecticut, where two officers were murdered by a gunman whose chosen
weapon for the ambush was an AR-15.
Petitioners’ arguments to invalidate Connecticut’s
AR-15 ban run contrary to history, precedent, and
logic.  According to petitioners, the Second Amendment categorically disables regulation of weapons as
soon as those weapons become commonly used.  That
rule would be a surprise to the lawmakers of the 1300s
through the 1900s, who often took action precisely because particular weapons became so popular as to pose
acute social problems.  And petitioners’ theory represents a “flawed” approach to constitutional doctrine
because it requires legislatures to “maximally exercise[] their power to regulate” or forever lose that regulatory authority.  Rahimi , 602 U.S. at 739- 40 (Barrett, J., concurring).  Indeed, the AR-15’s history itself
vividly illustrates the problems with petitioners’  rule.
On petitioners’ account, the 1994 Congress had authority to ban AR -15s before they were commonly
owned, but the 2004 Congress forever disabled future
regulation—at both the federal and state levels —by
letting that ban lapse.  The Second Amendment d oes
not create that one-way ratchet.
In short, the Constitution does not prevent Connecticut from banning the very weapons that have
wrought incalculable harm and unimaginable loss on
the people of that State.  This Court should affirm the
judgment below.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. Factual Background
1.  On December 14, 2012, a young man armed with
a lawfully purchased AR -15-style semiautomatic rifle
called the Bushmaster Model XM15-E2S shot his way

4
into Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut.  The amateur shooter fired 154 rounds in under five minutes, killing 20 first -graders and six
adults.  The shooter then turned the weapon on himself.
Police responded immediately but were too late to
intervene.  Upon entering the school, police encountered carnage so incomprehensible that one sergeant
recalled being unable to count the number of dead because “[his] mind would not count beyond the low
teens.”  Silvia Foster -Frau et al., Terror on Repeat ,
Wash. Post (Nov. 16, 2023).  A state trooper mistook
one of the classrooms for an art room because he
thought he saw red paint on the walls, until he “realized that the red paint was actually blood.”  See id.  Police found the shooter’s rifle near his body and the bodies of his victims.
2.  Within months, the Connecticut legislature responded to the mass shooting by enacting a bipartisan
law that expanded upon Connecticut’s longstanding
firearms restrictions and banned large-capacity magazines.
As relevant here, the law made two significant
changes to Connecticut’s preexisting ban on the sale,
transfer, and possession of “assault weapons.”  First,
it added the AR -15 and Bushmaster Model XM15,
among other firearms, to the list of banned weapons.
2013 Conn. Pub. Acts 13- 3 § 25(1)(B).  Second, to prevent manufacturers from evading the ban by renaming
their weapons, the law defined prohibited “assault
weapons” to include any semiautomatic, centerfire rifle capable of accepting a detachable magazine with at
least one of the following features: (1) a folding or telescoping stock, (2) any grip that allows the shooter to

5
hold the weapon so that the trigger -finger hand is positioned below any portion of the firing action, (3) a forward pistol grip, (4) a flash suppressor, or (5) a grenade
or flare launcher.  Id. § 25(1)(E)(i); see Conn. Gen. Stat.
§ 53-202a(1)(E)(i).  The statute permits owners of existing weapons to obtain “certificate[s] of possession”
that allow them to continue to lawfully possess their
firearms.  Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 53-202c(c)-(f), 53-202d.
B. Proceedings Below
Petitioners in Grant v. Higgins , No. 25 -566, are
nonprofit organizations and individuals who want to
own AR-15s or other assault weapons banned in Connecticut.  Petitioners sued various Connecticut officials and sought a preliminary injunction against enforcement of Connecticut’s assaul t-weapons restrictions.
The district court denied a preliminary injunction.
Grant Pet. App. 74a -92a.  The court explained that
Connecticut’s law is “consistent with the nation’s history and tradition of firearm regulation” because it targets “new and dangerous characteristics of developing
weapons technology.”  Id. at 90a.
The Second Circuit affirmed.  Grant Pet. App. 1a-
66a.  The court first rejected petitioners’ argument
that “the Second Amendment necessarily protects all
weapons in common use.”  Id. at 30a.  The court then
examined the “historical tradition” of firearms regulation and determined that it “encompasses those arms
that legislators determined were unusually dangerous
because of their characteristics.”  Id. at 31a; see id. at
67a-73a (Nathan, J., concurring).  The court explained
that Connecticut’s law was “  ‘relevantly similar’ … to
historical antecedents that imposed targeted restrictions on unusually dangerous weapons,” while

6
still “preserv[ing ] alternative avenues for the legal
possession of less inherently dangerous arms.”  Id. at
37a.  Thus, the court concluded that the Second
Amendment does not prevent Connecticut from “implement[ing] targeted regulations designed to protect
residents and their children from experiencing tragedies like the one at Sandy Hook Elementary School.”
Id. at 61a.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The S econd Amendment does not preclude Connecticut from banning an unusually dangerous
weapon that has inflicted incalculable harm in the
State.
I.  Connecticut’s ban on AR -15s falls within a long
historical tradition of governments regulating weapons unusually capable of causing death and destruction.
A.  For centuries, legislatures have made choices
similar to Connecticut’s, regulating weapons that pose
unusual dangers to the community.  The history  runs
in an unbroken line from medieval England to the
Founding to the Reconstruction era to the twentieth
century.  It begins with bans on the medieval
launcegay, an “immensely popular” weapon that was
unusually “responsible for fatalities.”  It continues
with English bans on crossbows, pocket dagges, and
steelets; colonial- era bans on trap guns and other
weapons; and nineteenth- century restrictions on
Bowie knives and other unusually dangerous arms.
That same concern with lethality later led to prohibitions on slungshots and Tommy guns.
B.  Like these other weapons that have been restricted throughout history, AR -15s are unusually
dangerous compared to their contemporary peers.  AR-

7
15s share the same basic structure and operation as
their military counterpart, the M-16, and are designed
to optimize sustained, rapid, accurate, and lethal fire
at long distances.  No other commercially available
weapon allows a shooter to inflict catastrophic injuries
on as many victims as quickly as the AR -15.  And the
AR-15’s technical capabilities are tragically borne out
in real -world experience.  AR -15s are disproportionately used in mass shootings: Gunmen have wielded
AR-15s in the deadliest mass shootings of the twentyfirst century, including in Newtown, Connecticut;
Uvalde, Texas; and Las Vegas, Nevada.  And AR- 15s
are distinctively dangerous to law enforcement: They
can penetrate police body armor and helmets, and they
have been used in deadly attacks on police officers and
other first responders.
C.  In all other respects, Connecticut’s regulation of
AR-15s is relevantly similar to its  precursors.  The
State’s ban on possession of AR -15-style weapons
matches the scope of historical bans of launcegays ,
Bowie knives, Tommy guns, and other unusually dangerous weapons.  And while other precursor laws regulated carry and not possession, this Court has previously drawn analogies between possession and carry
bans.  Dramatic technological changes—which allow a
single amateur shooter to rapidly kill dozens of individuals—further support the link between Connecticut’s law and its predecessors.
II.  Petitioners’ contrary argument—that legislatures are categorically disabled from regulating weaponry in “common use”—defies history, precedent, and
logic.
A.  No historical source supports petitioners’ common-use-only test.  On the contrary, English and

8
American history is replete with examples of governments banning excessively lethal weapons precisely
because they had become so popular that they posed
immediate dangers to society.  The launcegay  and
Bowie knife, for example, were both in common use
when restricted.  And none of the nineteenth -century
decisions discussing weapons restrictions held that
legislatures lost regulatory authority once a weapon
was in common use.  Instead, the historical record supports the notion that States have authority to regulate
weapons that pose unusual danger to their communities—even if those weapons are lawful, and even commonly owned, elsewhere in the country.
B.  The common -use-only approach also conflicts
with this Court’s precedents.  The Court has made
clear that the Second Amendment protects stun guns
but not fully automatic machineguns, even though
those weapons are owned at comparable rates.  It follows t hat something other than commonality separates stun guns and machineguns —specifically, that
machineguns are unusually dangerous.
C.  Finally, the common -use-only approach represents an illogical and unworkable approach to constitutional law.  Legislatures do not always maximally
exercise their regulatory power, and this Court has repeatedly rejected a use -it-or-lose-it view of legislative
authority.  Indeed, there is no other area of constitutional law where the choices of market actors permanently disable legislatures from passing laws to protect their communities.  And the common-use-only approach is neither administrable nor capable of principled application.  For example, it suggests that AR-15s
could permissibly be regulated in 1994, when Congress
enacted a federal ban—but that Congress’s choice not
to extend that ban in 2004 forever prevented future

9
legislatures from responding to the weapon’s unusual
lethality.  That single legislative choice does not forever determine the meaning of the Second Amendment.
ARGUMENT
I. Connecticut’s AR -15 Ban Falls Within A
Historical Tradition Of Regulating Unusually
Dangerous Weapons.
The Second Amendment provides that “the right of
the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.”  Because the Amendment “codified a right ‘inherited from our English ancestors, ’ ” District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570, 592, 599 (2008), this
Court has adopted a “historical approach” to its interpretation, N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597
U.S. 1, 24 (2022).  To sustain a law under this inquiry,
the government must “justify its regulation by demonstrating that it is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”  Id.
Connecticut’s ban is consistent with nearly eight
centuries of tradition.  From the 1300s to the present,
English and American jurisdictions have banned
weapons because they posed unusual dangers relative
to other weapons of the era.  And the AR-15 is the signal example of an unusually dangerous weapon today
given its unprecedented lethality and frequent use in
mass-casualty events and law -enforcement killings.
Accordingly, “  ‘historical precedent’ from before, during, and even after the founding evinces a comparable
tradition of regulation.”  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27 (quoting
Heller, 554 U.S. at 631).

10
A. The Second Amendment permits States to
regulate unusually dangerous weapons.
As numerous courts of appeals have concluded, a
wealth of “historical regulations impos[ed] targeted restrictions on weapons whose danger and lethality
stand out.”  Barnett v. Raoul , 180 F.4th 1035, 1047
(7th Cir. 2026); see Ocean State Tactical, LLC v. Rhode
Island, 95 F.4th 38, 44- 52 (1st Cir. 2024); Bianchi v.
Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 464-72 (4th Cir. 2024) (en banc);
Duncan v. Bonta, 133 F.4th 852, 874-84 (9th Cir. 2025)
(en banc); Hanson v. District of Columbia , 120 F.4th
223, 234-40 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (per curiam); Grant Pet.
App. 51a-61a.  Over the centuries, the march of technological advancement has increased the lethality of
weapons, and governments have consistently responded by outlawing weapons with characteristics
that make them more lethal than their contemporary
peers.  Those regulations originated in medieval England, traveled to America before the Founding, and
have persisted for the entirety of the American experiment.
1. English laws regulated unusually dangerous
weapons.
From at least the fourteenth century until the
Founding era, English laws prohibited the possession
of unusually dangerous weapons.  That “long, unbroken line of common -law precedent stretching from
Bracton to Blackstone” illuminates the Second Amendment’s scope.  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 35.
a.  England’s regulation of unusually dangerous
weapons “trace[s] [its] origin to the Statute of Northampton.”  United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 697
(2024).  The Statute provided that “no man great nor
small” may “bring … force in affray of the peace, nor to

11
go nor ride armed by night nor by day.”  Statute of
Northampton, 2 Edw. 3, c. 3 (1328).  The Statute codified the common-law crime of affray, or “terrifying the
good people of the land.”  4 William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England  148-49 ( 4th ed.
1770).  Although affrays often involved “fighting …  in
a public place,” a person could also cause an affray
without “actual Violence” by “arm[ing] himself with
dangerous and unusual weapons” as would “naturally
cause a Terror to the people.”  John Dunlap, The New-
York Justice 8 (1815); 1 William Hawkins, A Treatise
of the Pleas of the Crown 135 (1716).  Thus, the Statute
was understood to prohibit weapons responsible for
“the great peril and continual fear and danger of the
King’s most loving subjects.”  C rossbows Act of 1541,
33 Hen. 8 c. 6 (1542).  And the Statute prohibited possessing such weapons even if a person “d[id] not break
the peace.”  Chune v. Piott (1615) 80 Eng. Rep. 1161,
1162 (KB).
b. The Statute’s prohibition on unusually dangerous weapons was reinforced in subsequent enactments
that banned specific weapons.  Some of these enactments stated that the specified weapons were already
“contrary to the Form of the Statute of Northampton.”
See, e.g., 7 Rich. 2, c. 13 (1383).  In each instance, the
weapons were restricted because they were unusually
dangerous.
Launcegays.  The first English statutes banning a
particular weapon applied to launcegays: light, ashen
lances with sharp points at both ends.  7 Rich. 2, c. 13;
20 Rich. 2, c. 1 (1396).  Launcegays had a “lethal reputation” in England and consequently were “surrounded with notoriety.”  Michael J. Harbinson, The
Lancegay and Associated Weapons, 20 J. Medieval Mil.
Hist. 137, 137, 157 (2022).  The launcegay’s lethality

12
derived from its “versatility.”  Id. at 162.  Launcegays
could be “deployed” with “celerity,” while “penetrat[ing] armor at close quarters” and “giving death at
a single blow.”  Id.  at 162, 171.  Someone armed with
a launcegay could “easily best those armed with a
sword and buckler,” and they remained “effective
weapon[s], even in an age of more sophisticated firearms.”  Id. at 157-58.
Launcegays were “used by all classes” and “immensely popular,” but, because of their lethality, they
were also favored “instrument[s] of lawlessness and
murder.”  Id. at 157.  Launcegays were eventually
banned following their use in a series of well -publicized murders and their “responsib[ility] for fatalities”

“175,977.”  Id.
The Court’s disparate treatment of machineguns
and stun guns cannot be reconciled on a common- useonly approach.  Unless the critical common-use threshold lies between 175,977 and 200,000, another consideration must separate machineguns and stun guns.
The only plausible one is unusual dangerousness: machineguns are “exceedingly dangerous” because they
can “kill dozens of people within a matter of seconds,”
Bridges, 150 F.4th at 527; stun guns pose no comparable danger.  Thus, this Court’s precedent already recognizes that lethality—not just commonality—carries
weight when determining whether firearms regulations comport with the Second Amendment.
C. Petitioners’ common-use-only approach is
conceptually infirm.
Petitioners’ common-use-only test is also theoretically unsound, doctrinally anomalous, and practically
unworkable.
1.  The common -use-only approach rests on the
“flawed” premise that “legislatures maximally exercise[] their power to regulate.”  Rahimi , 602 U.S. at
739-40 (Barrett, J., concurring).  A responsible legislature takes time to “assess” the wisdom of regulations,
enacting statutes only after “observation and experience” confirm that legislation is appropriate.  Bianchi,

46
111 F.4th at 461.  Connecticut, for example, passed its
current AR-15 ban only after the Sandy Hook tragedy.
See supra at 3-4.  The common-use-only view penalizes
States for engaging in this deliberative process and
would ensure that “arms manufacturers can secure
constitutional immunity for their products so long as
they distribute a sufficient quantity” of arms before
the excessive lethality of those weapons becomes clear.
Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 461.
This Court has long held that a measured lawmaking process is not a source of constitutional infirmity.
There is no “adverse -possession theory” of constitutional law.  NLRB v. Noel Canning, 573 U.S. 513, 615
(2014) (Scalia, J., concurring in the judgment).  As this
Court recently held, “the fact that many States in the
late 18th and early 19th century did not criminalize
pre-quickening abortions does not mean that anyone
thought the States lacked the authority to do so.”
Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Org. , 597 U.S. 215,
253 (2022).  Likewise, there is no one-way-ratchet doctrine under the Second Amendment; the fact that some
States deliberated before banning AR -15s, and others
have not enacted restrictions, does not mean that all
States have forever lost their authority to regulate.
The Court should reject petitioners’ “  ‘use it or lose it’
view of legislative authority.”  Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 740
(Barrett, J., concurring).
2. No other constitutional provision supports petitioners’ common-use-only theory of the Second Amendment.  Under the First Amendment, for example, even
the most “widely used” speech platforms may be regulated to advance important state interests.  TikTok,
Inc. v. Garland, 604 U.S. 56, 71, 78 (2025).  There is no
other constitutional doctrine where the market choices
of private actors forever disable the democratic

47
process—and the Second Amendment is not “subject to
an entirely different body of rules than the other Bill
of Rights guarantees.”  McDonald v. City of Chicago ,
561 U.S. 742, 780 (2010).
Petitioners make no effort to align their test with
any other constitutional doctrine; the federal government, while taking up the challenge, fails to meet it.
See U.S. Br. 16.  The government primarily discusses
First Amendment obscenity doctrine; the Fourth
Amendment’s warrant requirement; and the truism
that “the common law itself is built on community customs.”  Id.  at 17.  But none of those doctrines allows
the commonality of a practice to prevent all regulation
by democratically accountable actors.  The upshot of
the Fourth Amendment’s reliance on “customary”
practice is simply that law enforcement must obtain a
warrant to search a house.  Id.  The result of speech
not being obscene is that ordinary First Amendment
scrutiny applies; moreover, the Court has rejected any
“fixed, uniform national standard[]” for obscenity precisely because “the people of Maine or Mississippi”
need not permit “condu ct found tolerable in Las Vegas,” Miller v. California , 413 U.S. 15, 30, 32 (1973).
And “common law rights” are “defeasible by statute.”
Alden v. Maine, 527 U.S. 706, 733 (1999).  In contrast,
petitioners’ proposed rule would make common use an
on-off switch that automatically disables legislation in
some parts of the country based on choices made in
others.
Nor is the federal government’s E ighth Amendment analogy persuasive.  The government suggests
that the Eighth Amendment’s meaning can turn on
“how many States have adopted a given type of law.”
U.S. Br. 19.  But the government’s cited opinion states
that even where the constitutional tex t uses the word

48
“unusual,” state “consensus is probative but not conclusive.”  Baze v. Rees, 553 U.S. 35, 53 (2008) (plurality
opinion of Roberts, C.J.).  And the Eighth Amendment
does not limit a State’s  mode of punishment due
simply to the “nose count of Americans for and
against” the technique.  Atkins v. Virginia , 536 U.S.
304, 343, 346 (2002) (Scalia, J., dissenting).  The Second Amendment is no different.
3.  Finally, the common -use-only approach yields
unworkable and absurd results —including with respect to AR-15s.
There are significant “concerns about the commonuse test’s administrability.”  U.S. Br. 18.  If 200,000
weapons suffices for common use, see Caetano , 577
U.S. at 420 (Alito, J., concurring in the judgment),
then a weapon is in common use if owned by 1 in every
1700 Americans.  It is difficult to see how such a statistic could reliably be measured.  See Graham Kalton,
Methods for Oversampling Rare Subpopulations in Social Surveys, 35 Survey Methodology 125, 125 (2009)
(discussing “major challenges in sample design” in
measuring “rare populations”).  Recognizing this problem, the federal government urges the Court to count
States rather than weapons.  See U.S. Br. 18-19.  But
the fact that petitioners and the government disagree
on how to measure common use simply underscores
the problems with their position.  In any event, the
government’s test is flawed on its own terms.  Here, for
instance, the 11 States that regulate AR-15s make up
35% of the Nation’s population.  See id.  at 20 & n.2.
Yet the federal government offers no principled reason
why the number of States that have banned AR-15s—
rather than the percentage of Americans who live in
those States—should be controlling.  See Bruen , 597

49
U.S. at 67 (discounting laws enacted by jurisdictions
with “minuscule … populations”).
Both petitioners’ and the federal government’s
counting methodologies are also unworkable because
they “base sweeping constitutional principles upon the
narrow experience of a few years.”  Atkins, 536 U.S. at
344 (Scalia, J., dissenting) (alterations omitted).  Consider the Bowie knife: Eight States or territories
passed Bowie knife restrictions before 1850; seven
more did before 1860; eight more did before 1870; and
twelve more did between 1870 a nd 1900.  Kopel &
Greenlee, supra, at 298-327.  It is bizarre to think that
Bowie knife laws were unconstitutional if challenged
in 1850 or 1860 but constitutional if challenged in 1870
or 1900.  But the common- use-only rule requires that
result.
Or consider the AR -15 itself.  Petitioners assert
that “approximately 26 million people[] currently own
at least one AR -15 or similar semiautomatic rifle.”
Pet’rs Br. 11.  But eleven years ago, “[r]oughly five million Americans own[ed] AR -style semiautoma tic rifles.”  Friedman v. City of Highland Park , 577 U.S.
1039, 1039 (2015) (Thomas, J., dissenting from the denial of certiorari).  And eleven years before that, “few
civilians owned AR -15s,” Bevis, 85 F.4th at 1199, because federal law prohibited “manufacture, transfer,
or possess[ion]” of the weapons between 1994 and
2004, see Pub. L. No. 103- 322, § 110102(a), 108 Stat.
1796, 1996-97 (1994).  Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in
2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common
use—and thus could be banned today.  But because a
single Congress made a single policy choice, AR -15s
are now in common use and cannot be regulated by any

50
federal or state legislature no matter how unusually
dangerous they have proven to be.
That result is nonsensical: The Second Amendment’s meaning is not forever fixed by the 108th Congress’s choice not to reauthorize the federal AR-15 ban.
The history of the AR -15 thus illustrates the “danger
in inferring a settled societal consensus from statistics”—and the even greater danger of letting those statistics become “frozen into con stitutional law.”
Thompson v. Oklahoma, 487 U.S. 815, 854- 55 (1988)
(O’Connor, J., concurring in the judgment).
*   *   *
In the end, petitioners have it right: “whether a
type of arm is too dangerous for ordinary Americans to
possess is one that the people are entitled to make.”
Pet’rs Br. 3.  The people of Connecticut, acting through
their representatives and in accordance with historical
tradition, decided after the Sandy Hook massacre that
AR-15s posed unacceptable dangers to the community.
The Second Amendment does not prohibit Connecticut
from banning an unusually dangerous weapon that
has caused untold harm and suffering within the
State.

51
CONCLUSION
The Court should affirm the judgment below.
